questions.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+3}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}})}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}}.$ Differentiating, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and compute it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+3}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}})}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\cdot \sqrt{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int \frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}} \\  & =\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{arsinh}⁡(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's rewrite our integral as

$$
\int \frac{21}{7-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=3\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{x}{\sqrt{7}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{artanh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{\sqrt{7}})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{\sqrt{7}}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{7}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and compute it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{21}{7-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =3\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{x}{\sqrt{7}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{7}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\sqrt{7}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{1-{u}^{2}} \\  & =3\sqrt{7}\operatorname{artanh}⁡u+C \\  & =3\sqrt{7}\operatorname{artanh}⁡(\frac{x}{\sqrt{7}})+C\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x}{\sqrt{7}}|<1.$

Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int_{4}^{2\sqrt{5}} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^2 - 4}}\, \textrm{d}x = \dfrac{1}{2}\int_{4}^{2\sqrt{5}} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\left(\frac {x}{2} \right)^2 - 1}} \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse hyperbolic cosine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{u^2-1}}\, \textrm{d}u = \arcosh{u}+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u^2$ as the variable, we have $\left(\dfrac {x}{2} \right)^2.$

So, let's substitute $u = \dfrac {x}{2}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{1}{2}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\textrm{d}x = 2\,\textrm{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $4$ | $2\sqrt{5}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $2$ | $\sqrt{5}$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\eqalign{
\int_{4}^{2\sqrt{5}} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^2 - 4}}\, \textrm{d}x &= \dfrac{1}{2}\int_{4}^{2\sqrt{5}} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\left(\frac {x}{2} \right)^2 - 1}} \, \textrm{d}x \[5pt]

&= \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{2}^{\sqrt 5} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{u^2 - 1}} \cdot (2 \, \textrm{d}u) \[5pt]

&= \int_{2}^{\sqrt 5} \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\sqrt{u^2 - 1}} \[5pt]

&= \arcosh u \Big|_{2}^{\sqrt 5} \[5pt]

&= \arcosh{\sqrt 5} - \arcosh{2} \[5pt]

&=  \ln\left(\sqrt 5 + \sqrt{\left(\sqrt 5\right)^2 - 1}\right) - \ln\left(2 + \sqrt{\left(2\right)^2 - 1}\right)  \[5pt]

&= \ln\left(2 + \sqrt{5}\right) -  \ln\left(2 + \sqrt{3}\right)  \[5pt]

& = \ln\left(\dfrac{2 + \sqrt{5}}{2 + \sqrt{3}}  \right)

}
$$
